title: 【Codex for CAD】4种Codex接入CAD方式！从MCP到Skill，实测计算+画图+改图的AI全流程，适用OpenClaw和Claude Code
text:
I’m He Jing, an Associate Professor at Beihang University;
the traditional workflow for construction
design in engineering
is quite fragmented.
Calculations use Lizheng, drawings use CAD,
and data gets typed in by hand—
but Codex can bridge that gap,
piping data straight from calculation docs into CAD drawings
to cut down on errors from manual entry.
Today, we’ll learn about Codex for CAD—
a tutorial covering both theory and
hands on practice—which also applies to other agents
like Openclaw and Claude Code.
While we’re using foundation pit support as our test case,
the findings can serve as a reference for other fields.
With traditional CAD,
drawing involved inputting commands or clicking icons,
manually defining points and distances.
Essentially, you were still manipulating the tool yourself.
But Codex does things differently:
you can say, “Draw me a row of piles
with an eight hundred millimeters diameter
and one point six meters spacing,”
and it will grasp your intent
and generate the graphic on its own.
Because Codex has been trained on tons of CAD domain data—
including scripts, macros, and so on—
it’s not just some tool that only churns out images.
it can grasp engineering terms like “pile diameter
eight hundred millimeters”
and then turn your descriptions into code that CAD can run.
Those in engineering design will relate:
during the calculation phase,
software spits out tons of data,
and you have to manually jot down key params onto drawings.
Botch one number, and that drawing must be redone.
In the drawing phase, for a mid sized pit,
you have over
a dozen cross
sections—each one involves nearly identical steps.
The revision phase is a pain:
if the client tweaks one parameter,
you have to manually update
all linked dimensions and rebar details.
And Codex is trying to solve the problems
in all three stages.
Codex links to CAD via four methods.
First, it can directly generate a DWG file.
Codex churns out a file
you can open in CAD
straight from your
description—super easy to get started with,
but its support for complex drawings is limited.
The second is to generate AutoLISP or Python scripts
which you then load and run in CAD.
This method aligns more closely with actual workflows,
and the scripts
can be saved
and reused—ideal for creating parametric templates.
Third, via the Model Context Protocol
to connect directly
to AutoCAD—this offers the highest degree of automation;
in theory, it can handle reading,
editing, and saving drawings all in one go,
but the setup hurdle is a bit higher.
Fourth: wrap the whole workflow up as a Skill.
It bundles layer specs,
common scripts, and prompt templates together,
letting Codex execute tasks
via a uniform
set of standards—ideal for in house standardization
within design institutes.
For this review, we didn’t just test one method;
we ran through all four
to see their respective scopes and limits.
Each review focused on different aspects.
the DWG method checks for output accuracy;
the script method checks if the code logic is sound;
and the MCP method
checks if its interaction with CAD is stable.
the Skill method tests if, once packaged,
it can truly be reused.
The “Skill” concept—put simply—is about setting
a fixed set of work norms
for the AI.
The most basic type is no code
Skills—input prompts, templates, layers,
naming, rules, and annotation needs.
so Codex sticks to this set of rules each time,
no need to re explain it each time.
Moving up, we have low code Skills,
which involve feeding in validated AutoLISP scripts
and Excel templates
that Codex can then call upon as needed.
The most complete one is the enterprise specific Skill,
which bundles all internal norms,
standards, component libraries, and common drafting workflows.
yielding a tailored capability for specific tasks,
such as a Foundation pit support CAD Skill
or a reinforcement drawing generation Skill.
Next up, we’ll walk you through practical examples
from three stages—calculation,
drawing, and revision—starting with the calculation phase.
Its overall performance is the steadiest of the three stages—
and why is easy to explain.
Calculation is essentially processing structured data:
parameters as inputs, numbers and tables as outputs,
with clear rules and verifiable solutions—tasks AI excels at.
From parameter extraction and layered calculations
to piecing together
a full calculation report—Codex handles it
all; outputs are formatted neatly,
and the process is traceable.
One detail bears noting:
the prompt must state clearly
that it’s not to fabricate things on its own,
and any missing content should be flagged for human review.
AI’s default behavior is to fill in blanks;
if you don’t tell it where NOT to fill in,
it will plug in a number that seems reasonable on its own.
Here, I’ll use an engineering calculation doc task
as an example;
say, I first upload a calculation doc.
Then, I send this prompt chunk to Codex.
Then, click send.
Okay! We can see the result has been generated
now; let’s check the desktop.
Okay! Here’s the complete foundation pit support calculation
document.
Next up is the drawing phase—this is where you can
most tangibly
feel the value of AI,
but it’s also where its limits are most apparent.
The parts it excels at center on
drawing tasks with strong, regular patterns.
Given params, generate geometric framework,
turn calc data into distribution plots,
and draw geologic sections based on soil layers.
What these tasks share is clear inputs and fixed rules;
Codex can handle them well,
and its output layer structure is quite neat.
The AutoLISP files generated via scripting
can also be saved
and used again
and again—essentially turning a one off prompt
into a reusable drawing tool.
By the way, for the same task,
using Claude Code to generate an AutoLISP
script works, too—and from my tests,
the code it spits out has even more thorough comments.
so if other teams need to maintain or tweak the script
later, readability could be better.
For slightly more complex scenarios—say,
adding anchor cables to an existing drawing,
or recreating a construction drawing
screenshot as a DWG file.
In that case, MCP
would be a
more fitting approach—it can read the original drawing,
pinpoint its entities, and draw within specific areas.
a workflow closer to reality than starting from scratch.
Especially for the task of recreating drawings,
many design institutes have tons of old paper drawings
or low res scanned copies on hand.
Without the DWG source files,
one used to have to trace drawings by hand;
now, AI assisted duplication can markedly speed things up,
but key dimensions still need to be checked manually
in the end.
Here’s a neat pattern: the three D schematic model.
two D construction drawings,
conversely, suit AI generation better as criteria differ.
For three D models, correct spatial relations are acceptable;
but for two D construction drawings,
every line's coordinates must be precise,
with far less tolerance.
Using three D models to explain shoring schemes
to clients or non experts works great,
but generating construction drawings directly from them?
Not feasible just yet.
Labeling norms and construction details
still need manual checking.
Mmm, first, we upload a construction drawing.
then send this prompt to Codex.
plus, I have AutoCAD open on my desktop.
Codex is now analyzing and connecting.
So now, we can see it’s drawn that construction
drawing in the CAD window on the right.
Next up is the revision phase—which boasts
the clearest boundaries
of the three stages.
Simply put: the simpler the task, the more stable Codex is;
but for tasks that demand a grasp of engineering logic,
it’s more prone to errors.
But overall, pinpoint edits to single drawing elements
are most reliable,
and local, linked edits can mostly be done.
But one thing to note: if the drawing lacks a clear scale,
it will measure things from the drawing itself
before offsetting,
so the actual accuracy needs to be checked by a human.
So, on my desktop right now, I have a file,
For this plan layout, I’ll send this prompt to Codex.
and send him the revision requests too.
Now, you can see it’s opened up
that Foundation pit support plan layout from my desktop.
Okay! Pocket X now shows it’s finished
that local, linked edit task.
After a look around, here’s my summary for you all.
Right now, the tasks best suited for Codex
are data collation and tabular output,
plus generating initial drafts of standard cross sections
and component diagrams.
text labeling, batch layer organization,
and pre drawing parameter consistency checks.
Since these tasks are highly routine and repetitive,
handing them to Codex can markedly save time.
But certain tasks still demand human judgment—for instance,
code applicability
and final calls on structural safety.
construction drawing standards
and cross drawing, linked edits.
AI can aid in collation and review,
but it cannot supplant
a registered engineer’s design duties—that line
must not be blurred.
This used foundation pit support
for testing—just a proof of concept example.
Plus, Codex for CAD’s core logic
applies across fields like architecture, structure,
municipal works, Maine P, and mechanical engineering.
For any scenarios involving parametric drawing,
turning calculation results into drawings,
or batch editing drawings,
this method can be ported over, too.
From this review, Codex for CAD’s long term value lies
not in single instance drawing output,
but rather in linking together calculation,
drawing, review, and revision
into a traceable, reusable workflow.
A few future paths to look forward to
include upgrading from generating files
to directly operating CAD via MCP.
from single point drawing tasks
to a full workflow of parsing calcs,
extracting params,
California D output, revisions, and diff explanations.
or by codifying design institutes’
internal expertise and norms
into bespoke Skills,
and shifting from passive drawing edits
to proactively checking for consistency and parameter gaps.

# Codex for CAD 知识图谱

## 整体工作流与 Codex 价值
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["传统 CAD 工作流"] --> B["计算阶段：大量数据输出"]
    A --> C["绘图阶段：手动输入参数"]
    A --> D["修订阶段：参数变更需手动更新"]
    B --> E["错误风险：手写记录"]
    C --> F["重复劳动：相似截面多次绘制"]
    D --> G["修订成本高：全局维度更新"]
    E --> H["Codex 介入：自动提取计算结果"]
    F --> H
    G --> H
    H --> I["降低错误率"]
    H --> J["提升效率"]
    I --> K["更可靠的设计交付"]
    J --> K
```

## 四种 Codex 与 CAD 的连接方式
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["DWG 文件生成"] --> B["直接打开 CAD"]
    B --> C["启动快，适合简单图形"]
    C --> D["复杂图形支持有限"]

    E["AutoLISP / Python 脚本"] --> F["加载至 CAD 运行"]
    F --> G["贴合实际工作流"]
    G --> H["可保存、复用，适合参数化模板"]

    I["Model Context Protocol (MCP)"] --> J["直接与 AutoCAD 通信"]
    J --> K["最高自动化程度：读/写/编辑"]
    K --> L["设置门槛较高"]

    M["Skill 包装"] --> N["统一层规范、脚本、模板"]
    N --> O["适用于机构内部标准化"]
    O --> P["可重复部署，降低重复说明成本"]
```

## Skill 层级结构
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Skill 类型"] --> B["无代码 Skill"]
    A --> C["低代码 Skill"]
    A --> D["企业级 Skill"]
    B --> E["包含提示、模板、图层、命名、规则"]
    C --> F["集成已验证的 AutoLISP 脚本"]
    C --> G["使用 Excel 模板"]
    D --> H["封装内部规范、组件库、工作流"]
    H --> I["面向特定任务（如基坑支护）"]
```

## 任务适配度与人工介入点
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["适合 Codex 的任务"] --> B["数据汇总与表格输出"]
    A --> C["标准截面、构件图的初稿生成"]
    A --> D["批量图层组织、文本标注"]
    A --> E["参数一致性检查"]
    F["不适合 Codex 的任务"] --> G["结构安全性最终判定"]
    F --> H["绘图标准、交叉编辑的细节把控"]
    G --> I["需工程师专业判断"]
    H --> I
```
